137-sara-crewe-or-what-happened-at-miss-:
Sara Crewe arrives at Miss Minchin's London seminary as a rich pupil, then loses everything when her father dies. Frances Hodgson Burnett's Sara Crewe, the early form of A Little Princess, follows the girl from privilege to attic drudgery. Miss Minchin turns her into a servant and mocks her pretenses.

Sara keeps her dignity by pretending she is a princess even in rags, and by kindness to Becky and the other servants. Her imagination turns cold rooms into stories and scraps into feasts. The tale ends with rescue and restored fortune. It became the seed of Burnett's most loved children's book.
13876-the-great-taboo:
Grant Allen published The Great Taboo as a romance of myth and adventure in the Pacific. Allen credits Frazer's Golden Bough for the central myth idea, plus Lang, Forbes, and Julian Thomas for other hints. Shipwrecked travellers land among islanders bound by taboo, ritual, and fear. A heroine in peril drives much of the action.

A wave strikes a vessel's flank and breaks in foam against her stern, in one vivid scene. Allen popularises Frazer's ideas on magic, kingship, and sacrifice through story. The novel mixes anthropology with romance and danger. Its Pacific setting feels lush and strange. Readers of Victorian adventure will enjoy its blend of science and story.
14313-one-of-the-28th-a-tale-of-waterloo:
G. A. Henty's One of the 28th follows Ralph Conway from country visits to Waterloo. Chapters promise unexpected news, a privateer's rendezvous, British cruisers, a commission, detachment duty, still-hunting, a cave among rocks, and a new housemaid. Belgium, Quatre Bras, Waterloo, and the rout close the tale, with illustrations from A. L. Burt's edition.

Home and war interleave. Mr. Penfold, determined after years without holiday, carries Mabel off to stay with Mrs. Conway, once his lover, now met without embarrassment like an old dear friend. His first words concern Ralph, grown quick and tall. Officers later debate winds: a fair west wind speeds transports across the Atlantic, while a foul wind might let Horse Guards stop the regiment in time. Henty writes boys' history with steady patriotism, and Waterloo arrives as earned climax, not mere backdrop.
14415-from-john-o-groats-to-land-s-end-o:
Robert and John Naylor walked the length of Britain in 1916, from John o' Groat's in the far north to Land's End in Cornwall, and wrote this day-by-day chronicle of the trek. Their route ran through Orkney, Shetland, and the whole island spine.

Entries record trains missed, storms at sea, Gretna Green marriages, village inns, and encounters with farmers, clergy, and fellow walkers. The brothers count miles, costs, and sights with cheerful stamina. The book is a classic of British pedestrian travel, full of local color from a country at war yet still open to two determined walkers.
18172-this-world-is-taboo:
Murray Leinster's science fiction novel follows Calhoun, a doctor of the Med Ship service, on a mission to a world long left alone. Calhoun drops out of overdrive near a banded sun, with the Milky Way seen from a strange angle. His companion is Murgatroyd, a small tormal who rides in a cubbyhole and greets the day with a shrill chee.

No Med Ship inspection has reached this world for twelve standard years, and the last was hardly an inspection at all. Calhoun expects to impress the natives with his animal friend and to grow unpopular himself as he checks their health. The novel turns on a planet cut off by taboo, and on what a lone doctor can learn when custom bars the way to plain facts.
18891-dot-and-the-kangaroo:
Ethel C. Pedley's Australian children's story, published by Angus and Robertson of Sydney in 1920 with nineteen illustrations by Frank P. Mahony, opens with little Dot lost in the bush. Sent to gather flowers near her cottage, she chases a hare and finds she can no longer see home.

Scratched and frightened under a great blackbutt tree, Dot is found by the kangaroo. The two travel among talking bush creatures, from the platypus and the kookaburra to a court of animals with a cockatoo judge. The tale ends, as its quoted reviews note, with Dot home again and the kangaroo's lost baby found. Pedley wrote for Australian children, hoping to win sympathy for the bush creatures facing extinction.
19177-hey-diddle-diddle-and-baby-bunting: Randolph Caldecott's picture book pairs two nursery rhymes with pictures. Hey Diddle Diddle brings the cat, the fiddle, the cow over the moon, and the dish with the spoon. Baby Bunting's father goes hunting. Only the rhymes and their pictures are present here. So the book is a brief rhyme book for very young children, not a story with a plot.
19668-skiddoo:
Hugh McHugh, the pen name of George V. Hobart, wrote this comic book of John Henry's opinions, published in Toronto in the early nineteen hundreds with pictures by Gordon H. Grant. John Henry holds forth on upper berths, cooks, patriotism, mosquitoes, streetcar manners, and chafing dishes.

One sketch sends a Dutch doctor and friends into a steel cage with rifles and smoked hams, waiting for foes of civilization. The humor is broad, slangy, and of its time, and the book shows the vaudeville voice that made John Henry a popular figure.
20515-the-eagle-of-the-empire-a-story-of:
Cyrus Townsend Brady's The Eagle of the Empire, published in 1915, is a novel of Waterloo. Its chapter titles promise a fast campaign tale. Readers meet bearers of evil tidings, marching armies, and the Emperor himself eating and riding toward his fate.

The hero Marteau bargains for a woman, meets Cossacks on the road, and stands a trial of allegiance. A rescue and a siege crowd the middle chapters. Brady, a clergyman turned adventure novelist, wrote the book for the centenary of the battle. It gives Napoleon's last campaign the pace of a boy's adventure story.
20741-the-adventures-of-a-dog-and-a-good:
A dog tells his own tale in The Adventures of a Dog, and a Good Dog Too. The narrator praises the plain speech of dogs over the bent speech of men. Dogs, he says, mean what their tone says, gruff or smooth, sharp or soft.

Through a dog's eyes, human pride and folly look fresh and odd. The book uses animal voice, a trick as old as fable, to mock human ways. Young readers get fun scenes, while older ones catch the satire in this warm animal tale. It is told as a story for the young.
23749-the-mythological-zoo:
Oliver Herford published The Mythological Zoo with Scribner's in 1912, a picture book of verse about creatures that never lived. Each beast gets a short, witty poem and an illustration, written to make young readers laugh while they learn the old stories.

The contents run from Medusa and the Siren through the Cockatrice, Cerberus, and the Sphinx to the Unicorn, the Satyr, and Pegasus. Medusa cannot do a thing with her hair of snakes, and the Siren is the chorus-lady of the sea. Herford's zoo is a gentle introduction to myth, best read aloud.
2389-bardelys-the-magnificent-being-an-a:
Rafael Sabatini's Bardelys the Magnificent sends a witty French nobleman into a wager: he must win a lady's heart without his fortune or his name. The swashbuckler moves through duels, disguises, and court intrigue in seventeenth century France, with Sabatini's brisk plotting keeping the swordplay and romance in balance. Bardelys himself is charming, reckless, and honorable.

The novel helped make Sabatini famous, and its hero anticipates his later rogues. Readers of historical adventure will find a stylish, fast-moving romance. It is pure entertainment, elegantly done. Sabatini later wrote Captain Blood and The Sea Hawk in the same swashbuckling vein.
28671-the-adventures-of-a-bear-and-a-gre:
Alfred Elwes's Adventures of a Bear, and a Great Bear Too, published by Addey and Company of London in 1853, opens in a bear's at-home. No carpets, curtains, fireside, pictures, or sofas await visitors, only soft moss or snow, spreading trees, tinted skies, romps, growling, and now and then a fight. Nine illustrations by Harrison Weir accompany the tale.

The bear is a big lump in a brown coat, always in a bad temper, while old Mr. Bruin sucks his paw in a corner. Elwes draws one moral from the den: good temper seasons every comfort, and its lack spoils luxury. Chapters follow travels, town life, prosperity, reverses, and rest. Young readers get a fable about temper.
32332-waterloo:
Hilaire Belloc's military history, published in London in 1912, treats Waterloo as a political campaign before it treats it as a battle. Belloc insists that general actions are functions of campaigns, and campaigns are functions of the political aims of governments. Until readers know what each side wanted to impose on the future, he argues, they cannot judge success or place a battle in history.

The book moves from the political object and effect of the campaign through Napoleon's advance across the Sambre to the decisive day of Friday, June 16, at Ligny and Quatre-Bras. It then follows the allied retreat and French advance on Waterloo and Wavre to the action itself. Clear maps of argument and movement make it a strong short study of 1815.
32518-the-adventures-of-a-cat-and-a-fine:
Alfred Elwes's Adventures of a Cat, published in London in 1857 with eight illustrations by Harrison Weir, presents a cat's biography drawn, the preface says, from the archives of Caneville. Elwes, author of Adventures of a Bear and Adventures of a Dog, chose the cat for a new subject. The celebrated Miss Minette Gattina, historian of poor Job, had bequeathed her memoirs to her native city with an introduction by herself. He converted those materials into the present form for young readers.

Elwes wonders whether the cat's true memoirs will win the favour given to his bear and dog tales. He also wonders whether they will match older feline favourites such as the strong-minded Puss who trod down boots in fairy tale. The book offers animal biography as entertainment, with a cat heroine, city manners, and gentle moralising. It suits readers interested in Victorian children's books and animal stories.
33022-villani-s-chronicle-being-selectio:
Giovanni Villani's Chronicle appears here in selections from the first nine books of his Croniche Fiorentine, translated by Rose E. Selfe and edited by Philip H. Wicksteed in a revised second edition of 1906. Villani, a Florentine merchant and chronicler, recorded his city's history, its wars, its trade, and its great men, and the editor chose passages that show Florence at its most vivid. Wicksteed compared the translation with the original and supplied the introduction and marginal notes to Dante.

The selections give English readers a medieval citizen's view of his own city, written close to events and full of detail about politics, money, and daily life. Selfe's translation keeps Villani's direct tone, while the indexes she prepared help readers find their way. For students of Florence, Dante's age, and medieval chronicle writing, this volume is an excellent doorway into a major source.
35677-education-in-the-home-the-kinderga:
Elizabeth P Peabody wrote Education in the Home, the Kindergarten, and the Primary School, lectures in the training schools for kindergarten teachers, issued at London in 1887. E Adelaide Manning wrote the introduction. A line from Froebel heads the book, come let us live with our children. Manning praises Peabody's work of twenty years.

Peabody helped spread knowledge of Froebel beyond his native country, Manning says. Owing to her efforts the value of the kindergarten was early recognised in the United States, she holds. First American promoters were encouraged by her to keep a high standard for teachers. Peabody was not content with merely intellectual methods, Manning notes. She aimed to train character and to grow mind and moral nature together. Children were to be prepared for the responsible duties of life, in her view.
3703-dot-and-the-kangaroo:
Ethel Pedley wrote this Australian children's tale to plead for the wild creatures of the bush. Little Dot loses her way among prickly shrubs, tears her dress, and sits down in fear as night draws on. A kind kangaroo takes her in hand and guides her home through the bush, and along the way Dot meets koalas, platypuses, and other native animals who can talk, grieve, and joke.

Each creature tells its own tale of hunger, hunting, and the loss of its young to guns and dogs. Dot learns to see the bush through animal eyes, and the book ends as a plea that children spare the gentle life of their own land. The story still charms young readers, and its plea for kindness to animals gives it weight beyond a simple ramble.
40029-the-gunpowder-plot-and-lord-mounte:
Henry Hawkes Spink, a solicitor of the Supreme Court, sets out to prove who wrote the famous warning letter that undid the Gunpowder Plot. His book came out at London and York in 1902.

Spink calls his case a proof with moral certitude, built like a court brief with questions, propositions, and proofs. Alongside the letter he gives an account of all thirteen conspirators, Guy Fawkes among them. His front pages quote Sir Edward Coke, who tried the eight men taken alive, on truth as the daughter of time. The letter to Lord Mounteagle has drawn guesses for three centuries, and Spink's volume is a lawyer's full-dress attempt to settle the authorship for good.
41214-totem-and-taboo:
Totem and Taboo is Sigmund Freud's study of the likenesses between the mental lives of savages and neurotics, as its subtitle runs. This English text is the authorized translation, issued in London by Kegan Paul. The front matter lists other new books on psycho-analysis, by Jung, Adler, and others. Freud applies his method to the customs of primitive peoples.

He treats the horror of incest, the rules of totem and taboo, and the roots of religion in the primal horde. The book argues that the fears and bans of early man match the fixations found in his patients. It remains the boldest of Freud's works on culture, and one of the most argued over.
42040-the-cruise-of-the-o-moo:
The Cruise of the O Moo is an adventure story for girls by Roy Snell. Reilly and Lee published the book at Chicago in 1922. The contents run to seventeen chapters. A front note points readers to page images kept by a university library.

Lucile Tucker wakes in her berth to a faint tapping in the dark. The sound comes again, hollow, as if beaten on a barrel head. A storm rises over the yacht O Moo while she listens in the black cabin. Her two companions sleep nearby, unseen behind closed shutters. Later chapters promise a blue face in the night and a trap in an old museum. A blue god, a phantom wireless, and an island's secret fill the cruise. Snell keeps the mystery moving for young readers.
44718-the-exiles-of-faloo:
Barry Pain wrote The Exiles of Faloo, a novel published by Methuen in London in March 1910 and reprinted the same month. Pain also wrote The Gifted Family. His island of Faloo lies somewhere in the warm seas, with surf in the distance, orange trees, and a French mission bell. A club of exiles keeps a broad verandah there, and native gardeners work the lawn in loin-cloths of tappa cloth.

Sir John Sweetling steps onto the verandah in the first chapter. He is fifty-five, tall, and inclined to stoutness, with a short white beard and fearless blue eyes. He scratches the club parrot's neck and calls it poor old Polly. The head gardener inspects the mowing from a resting position, wearing a splendid but unclean evening waistcoat. Pain settles into a comic portrait of Europeans idling in the tropics, far from the lives they left.
45027-chaucer-s-works-volume-3-the-house:
Walter Skeat, professor of Anglo-Saxon at Cambridge, edited this third volume of the complete works of Geoffrey Chaucer from many manuscripts. The Clarendon Press at Oxford issued the second edition in 1900. A plate from the Fairfax manuscript of the Legend of Good Women serves as frontispiece.

The volume holds three works. The House of Fame and the Legend of Good Women stand first, the two great dream poems of Chaucer's middle years. Then comes the Treatise on the Astrolabe, his manual of the instrument, with plates that show its parts. An account of the sources of the Canterbury Tales closes the volume. Skeat's spelling marks and notes keep the old text readable for students, and a companion volume holds the glossary. Readers get Chaucer the dreamer and Chaucer the astronomer in one scholarly dress.
45610-little-pilgrimages-among-the-men-w:
Little Pilgrimages Among the Men Who Have Written Famous Books is a set of sketches by Harkins. Page of Boston issued it, with copyright in 1901. A twin volume treats women writers of fame. Howells leads the contents, fronted by his portrait. Bret Harte, Mark Twain, and Lew Wallace follow. Cable, Henry James, and Stockton come next. Harris of Uncle Remus fame stands among them.

Mitchell, Crawford, and Allen fill the middle. Davis, Bangs, and Garland bring the list up to date. Each sketch visits the man at his work. Habits, homes, and methods are the fare. Such books fed the public's hunger for authors. The American writer was then a new kind of hero. Harkins writes as a pilgrim at shrines of print.
46159-two-in-a-zoo:
Curtis Dunham and Oliver Herford wrote Two in a Zoo, a book of zoo tales with art by Herford, issued at Indianapolis in 1904. The first tale sings the song of a captive elephant named Mahmoud. He stands in the Elephant House with an iron band clasped above one great forefoot, chained to a ring in the floor.

Mahmoud scorns his fresh hay and surges back till the chain creaks, with tears in his dim old eyes. His mate Duchess eats at his side and strokes his furrowed cheek with her trunk to soothe him. Other plates and tales bring in a princess, a limping boy, a hippo calf on its mother's broad nose, and a rabbit with one ear up.
49517-theatrical-and-circus-life-or-secr:
Theatrical and Circus Life, by John Jennings and published at Chicago in 1886, pulls back the curtain on stage and circus. Its full title promises secrets of the stage, green room, and sawdust arena. A history of the theatre from the time of Shakespeare to the present day forms one large part. Tales of the most famed actors and actresses fill much of the rest.

A full account shows how grand scenic and other effects are made behind the scenes. The origin and growth of minstrelsy gets its own treatment in the volume. The most startling tricks of modern magicians are laid bare for curious readers. A history of the hippodrome rounds out the plan. Many engravings and fine coloured plates grace the book.
49875-the-history-of-the-2-6th-rifle-bat:
The History of the 2/6th Rifle Battalion was printed in 1920. Gale and Polden produced it at Aldershot for the regimental committee. The battalion was the King's, the Liverpool Regiment, in 1914 to 1919. Captain Wurtzburg, its adjutant for two years, wrote the history. General Barnes, late commander of the 57th Division, adds a foreword. A dedication names Colonel Fletcher and the officers and riflemen who fell. Ten chapters trace the battalion. Formation takes it through Blackpool, Canterbury, and Margate. Overseas service begins at Strazeele and Fleurbaix. Armentieres and a gas attack fill the middle chapters.

Passchendaele is fought twice; Cambrai gets a chapter alone. The armistice finds the men at Lille and Arras. Appendices roll every officer and man by name. Photographs of officers and battalion groups face the text.
50302-the-rise-and-fall-of-nauvoo:
Roberts, an elder of the Latter-day Saints, wrote a history of Nauvoo dated 1900 as a mate to his book on wrongs in Missouri. He aimed to put the full tale of pain borne by the first Saints in the hands of the young. Faith made dear by the cost of those who came first is his hope for the book.

Chapters trace how the exiles were met in Illinois, the land buys at Commerce, and strife in town and state. The temple, the Nauvoo House, and the Nauvoo Legion mark the rise of the city. Trials of the Prophet, claims for wrongs, and fresh threats from Missouri drive the tale to its fall.
51865-the-lost-fruits-of-waterloo:
The Lost Fruits of Waterloo is a past study by Bassett. He wrote a life of a great chief and a short tale of the free states. It came out at New York and London in the spring of the last war year. Its rights were held that year, with all rights kept. Its first parts name its theme in plain terms.

First comes the ask of a peace that lasts. Then come the first plea hands for a peace of all lands. The fruits it means are the hopes that died with the great war of the past age. That war ended in the old ways, it holds. No league of lands was made then. The chance was lost for a full age, and the new war is the price.
53533-motor-matt-s-double-trouble-or-the:
Motor Matt’s Double Trouble, or The Last of the Hoodoo, is a dime tale of motors. Street and Smith issued it in New York on October second, nineteen hundred nine. It stands as number thirty two of the weekly Motor Stories, at five cents.

Matt King, called Motor Matt, heads the cast of young dare devils. Joe McGlory, a cowboy lad of worth and jokes, rides at his side. Tsan Ti, a mandarin of the red button, calls Matt to his aid. Sam Wing, a Canton bazaar man, works ill from his dark thoughts. Philo Grattan, a rogue of fine gifts, plots to steal a fortune. His theft of a motor car brings the law down on his head at last. Neb Hogan’s lost mule plays a great part in the wild chase. A red jewel and a sprung trap drive the tale to its end.
54908-historical-record-of-the-thirteent:
Historical Record of the Thirteenth Regiment of Light Dragoons is an official regimental history of the British army. It belongs to the Historical Records series ordered from the Horse Guards in 1836. A general order of 1 January that year, quoted at the front, commands the publication. The king wished an account of the services of every regiment to be published under the adjutant general.

The order lists what each account shall contain for its regiment in the series. It names the period and circumstances of the original formation of the regiment. It names the battles, sieges, and other military operations in which it has been engaged in war. This volume applies that scheme to a light dragoon regiment of the line, in the plain, dated style of the official record.
59273-discovering-evelina-an-old-fashion:
Frankfort Moore's Discovering Evelina, an old-fashioned romance, was published by Doran at New York in 1913. It stands as companion book to The Jessamy Bride. The scene is the Burney household in Saint Martin's Street, off Leicester Fields. Doctor Burney, the music master, lingers over breakfast before a noon lesson at the Streatham house of Thrale the brewer. His wife questions whether Garrick's influence on such a family is healthy. Fanny Burney glances up from her work basket with something of fright.

Doctor Burney laughs that Garrick's influence is like the air of the age, not to be resisted. The romance turns on the Burneys' gifted daughter and the writing the town has not yet seen. Moore builds his period tale from the real circle of the Burneys and their famous friends.
61790-my-literary-zoo:
My Literary Zoo, by Kate Sanborn, author of Adopting an Abandoned Farm and A Truthful Woman in Southern California, was published by Appleton in New York in 1896. Four heads divide the contents: Everybody's Pets, Devoted to Dogs, Cats, and All Sorts.

The opening chapter fixes the subject. Not the human pets of noted persons, Sanborn writes, such as Walter Scott's little Marjorie or Bettina von Arnim with Goethe. Her zoo holds the dumb favourites of distinguished men and women. A few pages go to tributes written to insects, birds, and animals with love, pity, or admiration, though not kept as pets. Burns's address to the mouse stands as the example: his apology that man's dominion has broken nature's social union. Press notices for Sanborn's earlier books fill the front pages, praising her eye for country humour.
66090-a-man-in-the-zoo:
David Garnett plays a strange game in A Man in the Zoo, printed at Toronto in 1924. The Macmillan Company of Canada made this Canada only edition, printed in England. Wood engravings by Garnett the elder dress the book. A note thanks Arthur Waley for a poem in his rendering, and clears the Royal Zoological Society of any slight.

The tale opens at the South Gate of the Zoological Society's Gardens. John Cromartie and Josephine Lackett give up their green tickets on a warm Sunday at the end of February. Spring smells mix with the odours of yaks, wolves, and musk oxen. The two are lovers, and they are having a quarrel. At the wolves and foxes they halt, and he rounds on her for always weighing the feelings of other people.
77902-moo-oo-oo-oo:
Laurence Donovan wrote this story of a city policeman and a lady in a roadster. A city policeman's official life may seldom be happy, the headnote at the front warns. Officer Corcoran, though, had some thrilling moments in his day's work, it promises in the same breath.

Even a hard-boiled traffic regulator may have his moments, the tale begins. Corcoran had four each weekday, standing at his crossing in the story. Shortly before nine each morning a silken little lady in a silky little roadster went by, her golden red bob the only view the smitten officer got at first passing.
bardelys-the-magnificent-being-an-accoun:
Rafael Sabatini set Bardelys the Magnificent in the France of Louis the Thirteenth, during a rebellion in Languedoc. Marcel de Saint-Pol, Marquis of Bardelys, wagers that he can win the hand of Roxalanne de Lavedan, whose family stands against the king. To woo her, Bardelys travels under a false name, is wounded, and is nursed in the very house he means to betray to fortune.

Sabatini piles up duels, a tribunal at Toulouse, eavesdropping, and a king's commissioner before the wager resolves. Bardelys narrates his own adventure with a rake's polish and a swordsman's pride. The novel is swashbuckling romance of the purest kind: honor, disguise, and love at cross purposes with a bet no gentleman should have made.
britannica-1911-bamboo:
Bamboo is the common name for a tribe of grasses, the Bambuseae, that grow large and often tree-like, with woody stems. The stems spring from an underground rootstock and crowd into dense clumps. The largest kinds reach 120 feet in height. Each stem is hollow, closed at the joints by a strong wall across it.

Branches are many and sometimes spiny, and the narrow leaf blade joins its sheath by a short stalk. The 1911 Britannica entry notes the odd flowering habit. Some kinds bloom each year. Others bloom only at gaps of many years, all plants of a kind over a wide area at once. One Indian kind was seen to flower at intervals of thirty-two years, after which the flowered stems die.
britannica-1911-cockatoo:
Cockatoos form a family of parrots, the Cacatuidae, marked by large size among Old World forms. A crest of feathers crowns the head, and the bird can raise or lower it at will. Green is absent from their colours. They live in the Indian Archipelago, New Guinea and Australia. They move in flocks and feed on seeds, fruit and insect larvae.

Their cry is harsh and not musical. Taken young, they tame well and grow familiar with people. Some kinds show marked sense, though their power to copy speech is small. The best known kind is the sulphur-crested cockatoo, white with a deep yellow crest. Flocks of 100 to 1,000 birds raid new-sown grain. Farmers thus destroy them without mercy. The small cockateel closes the account.
britannica-1911-cuckoo:
The cuckoo, Cuculus canorus, is a well-known bird whose name echoes its cry in tongue after tongue. In parts of Britain it is called the gowk. No bird, the entry says, has drawn more notice or more idle tales. Its strange habit of leaving its young to foster-parents drives much of that interest. The cock's cry, a true song of the mating season, announces its spring arrival in Europe.

The cuckoo summers across Europe, even within the Arctic circle, and winters in Africa. Small birds mob it on sight, mistaking its hawk-like flight and look for a bird of prey. In truth it is a harmless eater of hairy caterpillars. The long entry follows its breeding habits and its kin at length. It ends with an aberrant kind whose females share one nest and rear their young in common. Alfred Newton's name signs the survey.
britannica-1911-kickapoo:
Kickapoo is a tribe article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a people of North American Indians of Algonquian stock. The name means, in their tongue, he moves about. When the French first met them, the Kickapoo lived in central Wisconsin. Later they moved down to the Ohio valley.

In 1852 a large band of the tribe went south to Texas and Mexico, where they gave the settlers much trouble for years. In 1873 the bulk of the Kickapoo were settled on their reservation in Oklahoma, where the article leaves them. Their whole number at the time of writing is given as some 800 people. Of those, about a third were still living in Mexico, apart from the main body on the reservation, a split that matches the wandering sense of the tribe's own name.
britannica-1911-taboo:
Taboo, also written tapu and tabu, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is Polynesian, and it names bans guarded by the force of religion or magic. As a verb it means to forbid. As an adjective it means forbidden, sacred, dangerous, or unclean. Forms of the word run through Polynesia, and matching terms appear in Melanesia, Malaysia, and Madagascar.

The article breaks the core idea in two. In true taboo, two notions that later ages pulled apart are joined: the sacred and the impure. The impurity is itself sacred, and it does not come from contact with common things. It carries no sense of right or wrong in itself. One writer defines it as a mark of a link with the gods, or of a thing set apart for sacred use alone.
britannica-1911-toungoo:
Toungoo, or Taung ngu, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a town and district in Lower Burma. The town stands on the right bank of the river Sittang, one hundred sixty six miles by rail north of Rangoon. Its population in 1901 was 15,837. From the fourteenth to the sixteenth century it was the capital of a free kingdom.

After the second Burmese War the town was a key frontier station, but its troops were withdrawn in 1893. The district covers 6,172 square miles and held 279,315 people in 1901. That count showed a rise of nearly a third in ten years. Three mountain ranges cross the district from north to south, most of them clothed in dense forest. The rest forms the upper valley of the Sittang, the district's only large river.
britannica-1911-tree-kangaroo:
Tree kangaroo is the name for any member of the marsupial genus Dendrolagus. Three species live in New Guinea, and a fourth lives in North Queensland. They differ much from the rest of their family, the Macropodidae. Tree kangaroos live chiefly in trees, not on the ground. They feed on bark, leaves, and fruit. Their hind limbs are shorter than those of the true kangaroos.

Their fore limbs are longer and stronger than in their ground kin, with strong, curved, sharp claws. The best known kind is Lumholtz's tree kangaroo, found in North Queensland. It was named for the man who found it, who told of it living high in the hills. It lives in the thick scrub of spots hard to reach. Local hunters hunt it with trained dingoes, and its flesh is much prized by them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-tong:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Tongerloo describes a Norbertine abbey near Antwerp. Giselbert founded it in 1128 for the Blessed Virgin. Giselbert gave the land and himself became a lay brother there. The first monks came from Antwerp's St. Michael's, led by Henry, who had joined St. Norbert against the Tanchelmite heresies.

St. Bernard of Clairvaux and Blessed Waltman, first Abbot of Antwerp, signed the foundation charter, and Cambrai's bishop gave the abbots synodal rights. From very small beginnings Tongerloo grew into one of Belgium's most important abbeys. Its spiritual and social influence reached across the Campine, then a wild district with scant provision for its scattered people's needs.
doe-osti-2998578-a-scalable-hardware-and:
Northeastern University's final report on award DE-EE0009154 delivers a public data set on heat pumps serving the power grid. Michael Kane led the Northeastern team, with the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, Packetized Energy, and Ecobee as partners. Grid-interactive buildings shift heating and cooling to help the grid, but models of how people react were guesswork. This project measured both the machines and the households.

Laboratory tests captured second-by-second power draws. One unit was a 3-ton single-speed heat pump rated SEER 16 with 15 kilowatts of backup heat. The other was a 2-ton two-stage air conditioner rated SEER 21, tested across outdoor and setpoint temperatures. Field work followed 25 homes across three climates through heating, cooling, and shoulder seasons, with 20 of the original homes continuing after an extension for strong participation. Surveys and behavior tracking complete the human half of the loop.
doe-osti-3007248-aerosol-effects-upon-co:
Final DOE report by Sonia Lasher-Trapp sums up a project on how tiny airborne particles shape thunderstorms and the cold pools of air that spread beneath them. Field data came from the CACTI campaign in Argentina, paired with detailed three-dimensional storm simulations. Cold pools matter because they can trigger and organize the next storms in a line.

Particles that seed cloud droplets, called CCN, can delay a storm's first rain and weaken its cold pool when they are plentiful. A new model method tracks ice-forming particles as raindrops collect them, and with that fix the storms proved more sensitive to CCN than to ice particles. Effects still depended strongly on storm type and setting.
doe-osti-3012136-vehicle-cycle-inventory:
A vehicle cycle inventory for Type C school buses and intracity transit buses is compiled by Ramsharan Pandey, Rakesh Krishnamoorthy Iyer, and Jarod Kelly of Argonne National Laboratory. The October 2025 report, ANL/ESIA-25/17, tabulates the materials that make up each bus type. Internal combustion and electric variants are inventoried side by side for life cycle analysis.

Material shares differ modestly between powertrains. Rubber accounts for about 6.6 percent of the combustion bus and 6.8 percent of the electric one. Average plastic rises from 6.4 to 6.9 percent in the electric variant. The tables break out steels, aluminium forms, copper alloys, glass, and magnet content.
doe-osti-3018940-a-streamlined-open-sour:
Ethan Peterson of MIT, with Paul K Romano, Patrick C Shriwise, and colleagues at Argonne, closed award DE-SC0022033 with this final report. The three-year Fusion Energy Sciences project ran from August 2021 to August 2024. Its goal was an open-source neutronics toolkit inside OpenMC, the Monte Carlo transport code. Headline achievement: particle tracking on unstructured tetrahedral meshes. OpenMC became the first open-source Monte Carlo code with that capability. Mesh weight windows for variance reduction were generalized to all mesh types.

Shutdown dose rate workflows were built and validated in both two-step and direct one-step forms. Verification used SINBAD benchmark experiments, including FNG and FNS cases. Performance jumped as well: up to 4.5 times faster on complex models such as ITER E-lite. On that model OpenMC tracked 530 neutrons per second against MCNP's 150 in the table. Fusion designers gain open tools where licensed codes once stood alone.
doe-osti-3409101-prototype-long-term-loa:
Dated August 2026, report NLR/TP-6A40-100951 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies describes a prototype tool for long-term power load forecasts. Elaine Hale was the lab contact. The work is Project 3 under CRADA number CRD-24-25166, done with Equinor modelers as users.

Design work covered input data sources and a data inspection screen. A test install package let Equinor staff try a basic working build. The tool should let users inspect and refine forecasts with their own project data. Global planners need such forecasts to judge where power demand will grow over many years.
dot-and-the-kangaroo:
Ethel C. Pedley wrote Dot and the Kangaroo for the children of Australia, hoping to win their sympathy for animals. Little Dot chases a hare while picking bush flowers and loses her cottage in the scrub. Night, hunger, and fear close in as she sits crying under a blackbutt tree. Pedley, an Australian writer and musician, turns bush danger into an animal tale.

A mother kangaroo finds Dot, comforts her, and offers the ride in her pouch. From that pocket Dot meets the bush world at animal height. Platypus, koala, and creatures appear, each with habits and grievances against humans. The kangaroo, who lost her baby, mothers the girl toward home and safety. Pedley's plea runs under the adventure: creatures feel fear and pain, and children can learn to spare them. Australian families have kept the book in print as a first bush story for more than a century.
from-john-o-groats-to-land-s-end-or-1372:
Two brothers, Robert and John Naylor, walked the length of Britain on foot. Their route ran 1372 miles from John o' Groat's to Land's End. This book is their day-by-day chronicle of the tour. It begins with the sea trip to the far north. Orkney and Shetland stops precede the walk itself.

The diary records each week's stages in detail. Castles, lochs, glens, and battlefields fill the Scottish weeks. Glencoe, Loch Lomond, and Stirling appear in turn. Farther south the brothers note villages and local lore. At Eyam they retell the plague story of 1665. The book mixes mileage, weather, inns, and history. It reads as a walking tour written by the walkers.
govdocs-archive_org-SmithGeorgeTheJewsAt:
In 1851 the Right Reverend George Smith, Bishop of Victoria, published his account of a mission of inquiry to the Jewish community at Kaifeng, China. He traveled for the London Society for Promoting Christianity Among the Jews, which wanted firsthand word of that distant colony.

Smith describes the synagogue at Kaifeng, its Torah scrolls, and the customs of a community that had lived in China for centuries with little outside contact. His party questioned local Jews and recorded what remained of their Hebrew learning. The narrative is a rare Western eyewitness report on one of the world's most isolated Jewish settlements.
govdocs-archive_org-russian-occultism-vo: Volume 2 of Russian Occultism turns to the fate of occultists under Stalin and to the research of Alexander Barchenko. Barchenko led expeditions and studies that drew Soviet state interest in the 1920s. Under Stalin, occult circles were repressed and their members arrested or shot. The volume gathers that history: secret knowledge pursued in secret, then crushed by a regime that tolerated no rivals.
govdocs-archive_org-the-zend-avesta-2nd-:
The Zend-Avesta is the scripture of Zoroastrianism, one of the world's oldest living religions. Part II, translated by James Darmesteter for the Sacred Books of the East series, gathers the Sirozahs, Yasts, and Nyayis.

These are hymns and prayers: praises of angels and heroes of the faith, calls to the days of the month, and short litanies for daily use. Darmesteter's translation made the texts readable for English students of religion. As a world classic, Part II shows Zoroastrian worship from inside, in the words its priests preserved for millennia.
hey-diddle-diddle-and-baby-bunting-r-cal: Randolph Caldecott drew the pictures for this small picture book for young children. The hosted text holds two short nursery rhymes. The first is Hey Diddle Diddle, with the cat, the cow, and the dish and spoon. The second is Baby Bunting, a brief lullaby about a father gone hunting for a rabbit skin to wrap the baby in. Caldecott's plates carry the rhymes page by page, the words set as captions to the art.
one-of-the-28th-a-tale-of-waterloo:
George Alfred Henty wrote this tale of the Waterloo campaign. A. L. Burt published the illustrated edition in New York. Henty also wrote Bonnie Prince Charlie and other boy's histories. Chapter one brings unexpected news to the hero. A country visit and a run-down ship follow.

Later chapters visit a privateer's rendezvous and British cruisers. The hero returns home, then gains a commission. Startling news and a visitor for Mr. Tallboys follow. Service on detachment closes the sample's contents list. Henty mixes real Napoleonic war detail with adventure. Young readers get courage, travel, and battle scenes.
podcast-tuckercarlson-0jwHNHCUROo:
A self-described Covid whistleblower sits with Tucker Carlson to argue that the pandemic era hid two scandals at once. One is officials who claimed to predict pandemics. The other is an alliance between the CIA and researcher Peter Daszak's organization, which tied American science to labs in China.

Carlson draws the guest through the funding trails and the roles of intelligence agencies in public health. The guest's account treats gain-of-function research and pandemic planning as a single story of hidden power. These are contested claims, presented here as the speakers make them, and the episode stands as a record of the argument rather than a verdict on it. Listeners skeptical of official Covid accounts will find their case made at full length.
podcast-tuckercarlson-2q6nzNj1wOo:
Tucker Carlson leads a probe into refugee charities he says hide a dark trade. The title charges that trafficking groups wear the mask of aid work. Migrants, he argues, pay the true price.

Carlson traces how money, buses, and border chaos feed the system. He claims helpers profit while claiming to rescue the weak. The episode names groups and routes, per his reporting. It aims to shock viewers who give to such causes in good faith. Listeners get an accusation in full, framed as a rescue story that hides a crime.
podcast-tuckercarlson-ISETUBf6aoo:
Russell Brand, the comedian turned broadcaster, joins Tucker Carlson for a wide conversation. Its announced subjects include his political fall and his conversations with God. They also include the people he says are trying to imprison him, and a run for mayor. Brand speaks as a man whose fame, legal troubles, and faith now occupy the same stage.

Carlson and Brand share a trajectory: mainstream celebrity, rupture, and reinvention as independent voices claiming persecution by the old order. Their talk moves between prayer and politics without changing gears. The legal matters hanging over Brand are his to describe here, and he describes them as a campaign against him. The episode preserves two of media's most theatrical converts comparing notes on God and grievance for an audience that follows both men closely.
sara-crewe-or-what-happened-at-miss-minc:
Frances Hodgson Burnett begins Sara Crewe by placing her young heroine at a strict London boarding school run by Miss Minchin. Sara arrives from India at eight years old, sent by her father after her mother's death. He had kept the girl with him until the hot climate began to harm her health.

Burnett lingers on the tall, dull house and on the brass plate naming it a select seminary for young ladies. Sara reads that plate each time she passes and, by twelve, blames her troubles on being neither select nor a lady. Before leaving, her father buys her silk dresses, velvet, cashmere, and plumed hats, gifts far too grand for school life. His sadness at parting, more than good sense, fills her wardrobe.
skiddoo: Hugh McHugh, the pen name used by George V. Hobart, wrote Skiddoo!, with pictures by Gordon H. Grant. The Toronto issue by the Copp, Clark Co. rests on a 1906 copyright held by the G. W. Dillingham Co. Hobart lists many earlier John Henry books on the title page. The contents begin with John Henry pieces on upper berths, on cooks, and on love of country.
the-great-taboo:
Grant Allen wrote The Great Taboo. His preface is signed from The Nook, Dorking, in October 1890. In it Allen owns a debt. The central mythological idea of the tale comes from J. G. Frazer's Golden Bough. He also names works by Andrew Lang, Forbes, and Julian Thomas. He adds, with dry humor, that he can find no moral in the narrative.

Chapter I, In Mid Pacific, opens with a cry: Man overboard! A lady is in the sea. She is Miss Ellis. Felix Thurstan finds himself in the dark water, he knows not how. A woman clings to him for dear life. He is too stunned and dazzled to tell how it all took place. Frazer's lore of taboo stands behind the island dangers to come.
this-world-is-taboo:
Murray Leinster's science fiction novel, published by Ace Books in New York, opens with a small medical ship leaving overdrive. Calhoun finds the stars strange because the Milky Way shows from an unfamiliar angle. A banded sun sits off to port, within sixty light-hours of his destination.

He wakes Murgatroyd, his small companion called a tormal, who answers with chee sounds. No medical inspection has visited this world in twelve years, and the last report was poor. Readers get a space voyage about medicine, isolation, and a planet whose people expect the inspector to become unpopular.
